title: Ekamuk
author: Nabwile Joyce
desc: Sweet millet-flour porridge, mixed cold and stirred into boiling water with sugar — the Ateso breakfast and evening drink, sometimes soured by a short ferment.
longDesc: Ekamuk is the Ateso name for sweet millet porridge, drunk at breakfast or in the evening and sometimes left to ferment for a tangy taste. It follows the universal Ugandan flour rule — cold water first, mixed smooth, then into boiling water — and the only thing that distinguishes it from the porridges further west is the sugar and the name. Teso food is very thinly documented, and this is one of the few dishes from the region with even a method.
steps: Mix the millet flour smooth into cold water.
Bring water to the boil in a saucepan.
Stir the cold slurry into the boiling water.
Cook, stirring continuously, until it thickens to a drinkable porridge.
Serve warm — or leave it to ferment for a day for a tangy version.
chefTips: Cold water first, mixed smooth. Millet flour into hot water gives you lumps you will never get out.
Stir continuously from the moment it goes in. Millet porridge lumps the instant you stop.
The sugar is the defining feature — ekamuk is the sweet one, and the same flour unsweetened and fermented becomes something else.
Leaving it to sit for a tangy taste is documented practice rather than an accident, and it is the same instinct that produces obushera.

No quantities are documented in any source. The documented finger millet porridge in UGA066 — 125 g of flour to 500 ml of cold water into 2 litres of boiling water, cooked 7 minutes — is the nearest usable guide, and it is a cross-reference rather than an attestation for ekamuk.
Milk or tamarind juice added at the end is traditional in the Ugandan millet porridges generally, and the tamarind version appears in this collection as UGA039.

Teso is the thinnest-documented solid-food region in Uganda after Karamoja. The only listing of Teso dishes I could find is a single pseudonymously bylined blog post, and the serious academic work on Teso catalogues over a hundred wild edible species with Ateso names while explicitly recording no dish names or preparation methods. Ironically, Teso's beer is far better documented than its food.
commonMistakes: Adding dry flour to boiling water.
Cooking it thick — this is a drink.
Adding the sugar at the start.
Fermenting it in the refrigerator, which stops it.
sources: Ekamuk is documented as an Ateso sweet millet-flour porridge with sugar, taken as a common breakfast or evening drink and sometimes fermented for a tangy taste. That description is from the Ateso material in the regional survey for this collection. No quantities, timings or method steps are given in any source reached, and none has been estimated.

The cold-slake-then-boiling-water method in the steps follows the documented Ugandan millet porridges — the Slow Food Uganda booklet's finger millet porridge, p7, which gives 125 g of flour mixed smooth into 500 ml of cold water, poured into 2 litres of boiling water and cooked about 7 minutes, and appears in this collection as UGA066. That is a cross-reference from a related dish, not an attestation for ekamuk.
The finger millet name akuma in Ateso, and tamarind as nkooge in the Teso region with its use to prepare millet meal in the Iteso subregion, are from the Slow Food Uganda booklet, pp7 and 47.

On the state of the record: the only listing of Teso dishes found anywhere is a single pseudonymously bylined entertainment-blog post, and the academic work on Teso food systems catalogues over a hundred wild edible species with Ateso folk names while explicitly not recording dish names or preparation methods.
storage: Best fresh. 2 days refrigerated, or leave it to sour deliberately.
reheating: Warm gently with a splash of water, stirring.
healthBenefits: Finger millet is exceptionally high in calcium for a grain, plus iron and methionine.
Naturally gluten-free and very low in fat.
Thin enough to drink, which suits the young, the elderly and the unwell.
The sugar is added to taste, so it is under your control.
culturalNote: That Teso's millet beer is documented in peer-reviewed papers while its everyday porridge is documented nowhere is a good illustration of how research attention lands. The grain is the same, the community is the same, and only one of the two got studied.
